newsitem.title: USA: Vegetable prices headed higher after Florida freeze.
newsitem.headline: Vegetable prices headed higher after Florida freeze.

text.p: An unexpected cold snap destroyed nearly $300 million worth of Florida's winter vegetable and fruit crop last weekend, boosting supermarket prices for consumers, officials said Friday.

Gov. Lawton Chiles asked the U.S. Agriculture Department to declare 20 Florida counties disaster areas after last weekend's hard freeze damaged winter vegetables and citrus crops throughout the state.
Temperatures fell as low as 19 degrees Fahrenheit in central and south Florida last weekend, causing "significant damage" to winter vegetables, citrus, pasture lands and nursery plants, Chiles said.
Miami's Dade County has estimated its vegetable losses at $95 million, and total statewide losses are likely to top $270 million, Chiles said.
The cold temperatures were the worst to hit Florida's $3 billion a year fruit and vegetable industry since a killer freeze in December, 1989.
More than 50 percent of south Florida's winter vegetable crop was damaged by the freeze, with hardest hit crops being tomatoes, green beans, squash, bell peppers, eggplant, sweet corn and zucchini.

Supermarkets in the eastern and midwestern states have already marked up some produce prices to reflect the diminished supply, with some items doubling in retail price since the weekend, officials sai.
"While citrus losses are still being assessed, early reports indicate 10 to 35 percent of the crop being affected in certain counties," the governor said in a letter to the Agriculture Department.
Florida citrus growers have been examining groves since last weekend to try and estimate the amount of damage to young trees and oranges yet to be harvested.

"Every day we're finding more damage in the citrus groves. But we won't have any specific damage estimates until the next monthly crop report comes out on Feb. 10," said Bobby McKown, head of Florida Citrus Mutual, the state's largest grower cooperative.
